content:
According to the Financial Times, the latest court documents reveal that OpenAI is disappointed with the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, stating that the integration has 'performed far below expectations' since its launch in 2024. Details are as follows.

OpenAI is asking the court to rule before trial

In August 2025, Elon Musk stated that X, which has now been merged into SpaceXAI, will sue Apple and OpenAI over alleged collusion to exclude competitors in the artificial intelligence sector. The dispute stems from OpenAI's agreement with Apple to integrate ChatGPT into Apple Intelligence and Siri.

After the lawsuit was formally filed, the actual scope of the allegations went beyond the App Store ranking issues that Musk had initially complained about publicly. X and SpaceXAI also accused Apple of attempting to hinder the development of 'super apps,' including X's efforts to transform itself into an 'everything app.'

Over the following weeks and months, the relevant companies filed briefs, allegations, and defences with the court. Apple and OpenAI have consistently argued that the agreement was not an exclusive partnership as alleged; meanwhile, the court documents have also revealed new details about how this collaboration operates behind the scenes.

One such detail was exposed today in a document submitted by OpenAI. According to a Financial Times report, OpenAI 'expressed disappointment at how little interest iPhone users showed after the two sides reached a deal in 2024 to let ChatGPT power Apple Intelligence.'

The report reads as follows:

Court documents filed on Wednesday pointed out that when the deal was reached in 2024, OpenAI had expected to generate a 'halo effect' from Apple's promotion and brand association, and to attract more Apple Intelligence users to subscribe. However, one month after the ChatGPT integration launched, the 'start appeared slow,' prompting OpenAI to lower its forecast for weekly active user growth. The documents also stated that by the summer of 2025, 'it had become clear that Apple's integration of ChatGPT had performed far below expectations.'

The report noted that today's filing contains several redacted passages of dialogue, but the unredacted portions show that OpenAI executives were concerned Apple might 'want to move faster' to lock in another AI partner.

When Apple Intelligence was first announced in 2024, Craig Federighi said in an interview that Apple ultimately hoped to give users the ability to choose between different AI models, explicitly mentioning Google Gemini as a potential future partner.

That particular partnership never materialised, but Apple subsequently turned to Google's Gemini model to help power the new Siri AI, while Xcode has also been expanded to support coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.

Top-liked comment by OliveCocktail

Just as others have said, when I want to use ChatGPT, I go straight to their standalone app. That's actually my preference, because I don't want to mix all my voice requests together. I'd rather have Apple handle my personalised, context-aware stuff. I've never really figured out the privacy implications of using the ChatGPT 'integration,' and I've never bothered to look into it because I know I won't use it. On the privacy front, by contrast, I'm very comfortable using Apple Intelligence/Siri.

Returning to today's filing, the Financial Times noted that the documents also point to the way Apple rolled out ChatGPT as possibly one of the reasons for the slow adoption, since the integration is off by default.

Finally, according to Reuters, OpenAI is also arguing that SpaceX's recent securities filings are sufficient to undermine SpaceXAI's claim that the Apple partnership harms competition. OpenAI stated in its filing that SpaceX's IPO registration statement 'is full of disclosures that are the exact opposite of the competitive harm alleged in the lawsuit.'

On these grounds, OpenAI is asking Judge Mark Pittman to rule in its favour on SpaceXAI's antitrust claims before trial. The case is currently scheduled for trial in January.
